title: Gray Code Generation
directAnswer: An n-bit Gray code is a sequence of all 2ⁿ numbers where consecutive entries differ in exactly one bit. The cleanest construction is the formula `gray(i) = i ^ (i >> 1)` for i from 0 to 2ⁿ - 1. XORing i with its own right-shift cancels all but the single-bit transitions, so each step flips exactly one bit. It runs in O(2ⁿ) time, one O(1) formula per element.

rules: `gray(i) = i ^ (i >> 1)` converts the i-th integer into the i-th Gray code directly.
The sequence has exactly `2ⁿ` entries and starts at 0 — that start is part of the spec.
Consecutive codes differ in **one bit**; so do the first and last (it's a cyclic / reflected code).
The recursive 'reflect' build is equivalent: mirror the list and prefix the new high bit with 1.
Don't confuse the index i with the code value — you iterate i, but you store i ^ (i >> 1).
whenToUse: Generating sequences where neighbors change in a single bit (hardware encoders, K-maps)
Minimizing switching when stepping through all bit patterns
Any 'list all 2ⁿ states, one-bit change between steps' construction
Mapping a counter to a glitch-free encoder value
antiSignals: Need all subsets in any order → plain 0..2ⁿ-1 bitmask enumeration, no Gray ordering
Need permutations, not bit patterns → backtracking, not Gray code
Need to decode Gray back to binary → cumulative XOR, a different formula
n is huge → 2ⁿ output is infeasible regardless of method
remember.takeaway: The Gray code formula `i ^ (i >> 1)` is the one-liner to memorize: it turns a normal counter into a one-bit-change-per-step sequence. The reflect-and-prefix recursion is the same idea built bottom-up.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know the i ^ (i >> 1) identity (or can derive the reflect construction) and understand why each step flips exactly one bit.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Storing the loop index i instead of the converted code i ^ (i >> 1), or building only 2ⁿ - 1 entries by an off-by-one in the loop bound.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Show the O(1)-per-element formula, explain why XOR with the shift isolates single-bit transitions, and mention the equivalent reflect-and-prefix recursion.

problemStatement:
An n-bit **Gray code sequence** is a sequence of `2ⁿ` integers where:

- Every integer is in the inclusive range `[0, 2ⁿ - 1]`,
- The first integer is `0`,
- An integer appears no more than once,
- The binary representations of every pair of **adjacent** integers differ by exactly **one bit**, and
- The binary representations of the **first** and **last** integers also differ by exactly one bit.

Given an integer `n`, return any valid n-bit Gray code sequence.
constraints: Multiple valid sequences exist; any correct one is accepted
understanding: Produce all 2ⁿ patterns of n bits, ordered so each consecutive pair (and the wrap-around pair) differs in a single bit. The list must start at 0. The standard reflected Gray code satisfies all of this, and the formula i ^ (i >> 1) generates exactly that ordering.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the sequence have to start at 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the spec fixes the first element at 0. The formula naturally starts there since 0 ^ 0 = 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the first and last also differ by one bit?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — it's a cyclic code. The reflected Gray code guarantees this wrap-around property automatically.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is any valid ordering accepted, or a specific one?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any valid Gray code is accepted. I'll return the canonical reflected one via i ^ (i >> 1).

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 16, so 2ⁿ is at most 65536 entries — generating the full list is fine.

examples.explanation: Binary 00, 01, 11, 10. Each adjacent pair flips one bit, and 10 → 00 (last to first) also flips one.
00→1 differs by one bit; wrap 1→0 also one bit.
Binary 000,001,011,010,110,111,101,100 — every step is a single-bit flip.

approaches.name: Reflect and Prefix (Constructive Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this if you don't recall the formula — it derives Gray code from its definition.
hints: Suppose you have a valid (n-1)-bit Gray code. How could you extend it to n bits while keeping the one-bit-change property?
Take the (n-1)-bit list, then append its reverse. The original half keeps a leading 0; the reflected half gets a leading 1.
At the mirror seam the two halves share the same lower bits, so only the new high bit changes — one bit. Start from [0] and repeat n times.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each doubling step processes the current list once; the list sizes are 1, 2, 4, …, 2ⁿ, summing to about 2ⁿ⁺¹. So total work and output are O(2ⁿ).
approaches.explanation:
Build the sequence by repeatedly mirroring and tagging a new high bit.

**Start small.** The 0-bit Gray code is `[0]`. To go from `k` bits to `k+1` bits, take the current list and its reverse.

**Reflect.** Write the current list as-is (these implicitly have a leading 0 in the new bit position), then write it again in reverse order with the new high bit set: add `1 << k` to each reflected element.

**Why one bit changes at the seam.** Within the first half, adjacency is inherited from the smaller valid code. Within the second half, it's the same code reversed, so adjacency still holds. At the boundary between the two halves, the lower bits are identical (it's a mirror) and only the freshly added high bit differs — exactly one bit. The wrap-around from last to first flips only that high bit too.

**Repeat n times.** After n doublings the list holds all 2ⁿ codes. This is literally the definition of the *reflected* Gray code, which is why the formula approach produces the same ordering.
approaches.insight: Reflection is what guarantees the single-bit seam: a mirrored copy shares lower bits at the join, so adding one new high bit is the only change. Recognizing 'mirror then prefix' as the generator demystifies the formula.

dryRun.intro: Start from [0]. Double twice, adding the new high bit to the reflected half.

pitfalls: Forgetting to reverse the reflected half — neighbors then differ by more than one bit.
Setting the wrong bit (using k+1 or n instead of k) when OR-ing the high bit.
Starting from an empty list instead of [0], breaking the required leading 0.

approaches.name: Direct Formula — i ^ (i >> 1) (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The crisp answer. Phrase it as 'the i-th Gray code is just i XOR (i shifted right by one)'.
hints: Is there a direct map from a plain counter value i to its Gray code, with no list-building?
Try gray(i) = i ^ (i >> 1). Compute it for i = 0,1,2,3 and compare bits with the reflected sequence.
Loop i from 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 and append i ^ (i >> 1). The output size 2ⁿ is unavoidable; the per-element work is O(1).
approaches.complexityReasoning: The loop runs 2ⁿ times, each iteration doing one shift and one XOR in O(1). Producing 2ⁿ outputs is the lower bound, so the formula is optimal; space is O(2ⁿ) for the result list.
approaches.explanation:
Map each counter value straight to its Gray code with one XOR.

**The formula.** The i-th reflected Gray code is `i ^ (i >> 1)`. You iterate i over the normal binary counter 0, 1, 2, …, 2ⁿ - 1 and convert each value on the fly.

**Why XOR with the shift gives one-bit steps.** In Gray code, bit `j` of `gray(i)` equals `bit_j(i) XOR bit_{j+1}(i)` — each Gray bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits, which is exactly what `i ^ (i >> 1)` computes. When the counter goes from `i` to `i + 1`, binary addition flips a run of low bits: the lowest 0 becomes 1 and the 1s below it become 0. After the XOR-with-shift, all those cascading flips cancel out in pairs, leaving precisely one changed bit between `gray(i)` and `gray(i + 1)`.

**Why it starts at 0 and wraps cleanly.** `gray(0) = 0 ^ 0 = 0`, satisfying the leading-0 requirement. The reflected code is cyclic, so `gray(2ⁿ - 1)` and `gray(0)` also differ in a single bit — the formula reproduces the same reflected ordering as the constructive build, so it inherits that wrap-around property.

**Store the code, not the index.** The classic slip is appending `i` instead of `i ^ (i >> 1)`. You loop over the index but emit the converted value.
approaches.insight: `i ^ (i >> 1)` works because each Gray bit is the parity of two neighboring binary bits. The carry cascade of incrementing a counter flips a contiguous block of bits, and XOR-ing with the shifted copy collapses that block to a single net change — that's the whole reason consecutive Gray codes are one bit apart.

code.python:
def grayCode(self, n: int) -> list[int]:
    return [i ^ (i >> 1) for i in range(1 << n)]

Convert the counter value i to its Gray code; store the code, never i itself.

diagrams.title: Counter i vs Gray code i ^ (i>>1)
diagrams.caption: Each Gray value differs from its neighbor in exactly one bit.

edgeCases.behavior: 1 << 0 = 1, loop runs once → [0]; a single code, trivially valid.
65536 entries; each still one shift + XOR, no overflow within int range.
gray(2ⁿ-1) differs from gray(0)=0 by one bit — the reflected code is cyclic.

pitfalls: Appending i instead of i ^ (i >> 1) — outputs plain binary, not Gray code.
Using i >> 1 with a signed shift on a negative i — not an issue here since i ≥ 0.
Off-by-one loop bound producing 2ⁿ - 1 or 2ⁿ + 1 entries.

commonMistakes: Returning the loop index i rather than the converted code i ^ (i >> 1).
Looping to 2ⁿ - 1 inclusive incorrectly, yielding the wrong element count.
Forgetting that the sequence must start at 0 and wrap around in a single bit.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Emitting the index instead of the Gray code
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Iterating i and appending i gives plain binary counting, where i=1 (01) to i=2 (10) flips two bits — not a Gray code.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return [i for i in range(1 << n)]  # plain binary, not Gray
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return [i ^ (i >> 1) for i in range(1 << n)]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reflection without reversal
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In the constructive build, appending the half forward instead of reversed breaks the single-bit seam, so adjacent codes can differ in multiple bits.

patternNote: Gray code construction: the formula i ^ (i >> 1) maps a counter to a one-bit-change sequence, and the reflect-and-prefix recursion builds the same reflected code. The bit-parity idea recurs in encoding and subset-enumeration problems.
